name: Ahilud
title: Father of Jehoshaphat and Baana, officials under David and Solomon
summary: Achilud is a biblical figure known exclusively through his two sons, both of whom held central offices in the united kingdom of Israel. Jehoshaphat, son of Achilud, served as royal recorder (Hebrew: mazkir) under kings David and Solomon—a role that likely encompassed far more than history-writing and can rather be compared to a chancellor or court herald. The other son, Baana, was one of Solomon’s twelve district governors responsible for an area that included the strategically important cities of Taanach and Megiddo. The Bible gives no direct information about Achilud himself, but his sons’ prominent positions at court testify that the family belonged to an influential class of officials who were crucial to the kingdom’s administration and governance.

footnotes.text: The name Ahilud (Hebrew: אֲחִילוּד, Achilud) likely means 'brother of one who was born' or 'my brother is born.' The construction of the name follows a common Semitic pattern with 'ach' (brother) as the first element and may reflect a family tradition in which the child is seen in relation to an older brother.

The role of 'mazkir' (מַזְכִּיר), often translated as 'chancellor' or 'royal recorder,' likely involved more than simply recording history. The position may have included functions such as master of ceremonies, herald, and advisor—comparable to similar roles in other ancient Near Eastern courts, such as the Egyptian title 'whm.w' (herald).

The lists of officials serving under David and Solomon in the books of Samuel and Kings reflect a well-developed bureaucratic structure with parallels in Egyptian and Mesopotamian administration. The fact that Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, served under both David and Solomon suggests that certain offices were hereditary or tied to specific families.

Solomon's division of the kingdom into twelve administrative districts represents a reform in which the deputies, including Baana son of Ahilud, were responsible for supplying the king's household one month at a time. Archaeological findings from Megiddo and other cities in the region confirm the administrative infrastructure that such offices presupposed.

The fact that two of Ahilud's sons held prominent positions in the kingdom's administration—Jehoshaphat as royal recorder and Baana as deputy—shows that certain families formed a class of officials in the united kingdom. This pattern is well known from other ancient Near Eastern societies, including Egypt and Assyria.
